structured_output.hypothesis: If Thompson is right, the two families of contact parastichies in sunflower capitula cross at a roughly constant angle across the disc (isogonal), and only a small minority of capitula or radial positions have crossing angles within a few degrees of 90 degrees.
structured_output.pass_criterion: In at least 30 capitula with floret coordinates, the crossing angle between the two parastichy families is constant across the disc. Its standard deviation within each capitulum, over radii from 0.3R to 0.9R, is at most 10 degrees. Fewer than 20% of capitula have a median crossing angle within 85-95 degrees. Both conditions must hold.
structured_output.fail_criterion: Either more than 50% of capitula have a median crossing angle within 85-95 degrees (orthogonality is common, as Church held), or the within-capitulum standard deviation of crossing angle exceeds 20 degrees in more than half of capitula (the angle is not constant).
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'spirals' are the visible contact parastichies, treated as logarithmic spirals around the capitulum centre. 'Isogonal' means a constant crossing angle along the curves. 'Orthogonal' means a 90-degree crossing, which Church argued is the normal case. Modern reinterpretation: the parastichies are computed from floret centre coordinates, using Vogel's model r=c*sqrt(n) with a divergence angle of about 137.5 degrees. The crossing angle is measured between the local tangents of the two families. Note that an Archimedean (Fermat) lattice is not strictly logarithmic, so the test checks near-constancy of angle against orthogonality and does not test exact logarithmic form.
structured_output.no_dataset_reason: I could not confirm any public dataset, with a verified landing page or DOI, that records floret or seed centre coordinates, or parastichy crossing angles, for sunflower capitula. GBIF, NCBI, Dryad and similar portals hold occurrence, genome and trait data, not per-capitulum floret geometry. Citing a specific paper's supplement from memory would risk a fabricated identifier, so I return null. The test would need either a new image set of sunflower heads with floret coordinates extracted, or a published coordinate dataset that I have not verified.
